action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
 - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
- Fast file pattern matching tool that works with any codebase size
- Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts"
- Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time
- Use this tool when you need to find files by name patterns
- When you are doing an open ended search that may require multiple rounds of globbing and grepping, use the Agent tool instead (if available)

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
  - Supports full regex syntax (e.g., "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+")
  - Filter files with glob parameter (e.g., "*.js", "**/*.tsx") or type parameter (e.g., "js", "py", "rust")
  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool (if available) for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)
  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
## Auto Mode Active

Bias toward working without stopping for clarifying questions — when you'd normally pause to check, make the reasonable call and keep going; they'll redirect you if needed. If the user, a skill, or the shape of the task suggests they want you to ask (with AskUserQuestion or otherwise), do so. And even absent that signal, it's still fine to stop when you're genuinely blocked — unclear direction, missing input, a decision only they can make.

Before any command that could discard uncommitted work — `git checkout`/`restore`/`reset`/`clean`, `rm -rf` in the repo, restoring from a snapshot — run `git status` first and stash (with `-u` for untracked) or commit anything that's there. When staging or committing, review what's included (`git status` after a broad `git add`), and if you see anything suspicious that might reveal secrets — even if the filename looks innocuous — double-check the file's contents before pushing.

{"number":230,"title":"Page: fixed frame, 1 cm footer with the site version","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01NLfVm5WfzHBRRyA4oMF5jh?thread=cmsg_01NLfVm5WfzHBRRyA4oMF5jhKUmZ1vDWkaHNc4R6fwWVq9)_

Before:
- In Ariel's browser the logo showed huge, the status bar was tall, and the whole page scrolled.
- Windows narrower than 1100 px stacked the columns.
- The site version was not shown anywhere.

After:
- The frame is fixed. The 52 px header, the three columns and a 1 cm footer fill the window exactly, and only the left bar, the main box and the right bar scroll. Narrower windows get narrower side bars instead of stacked columns.
- The logo is 36 px high inside the header.
- The footer ends with the site version, e.g. "v1.0.0". It shows 1.0.0 until the first release after this merges.

Stale files: after the last release, a browser could keep the previous stylesheet for a few minutes and show it with the new page. The old stylesheet had no rule for the logo, and I infer that is why it showed huge; I did not reproduce it. The service worker now revalidates the site's own files on every load.

How:
- The public-website pack is adopted. It owns the version scheme and the page stamp, and the github-pages release already bumps the version when this pack is declared.
- `package.json` is the version record. The footer's `title="version …"` is the stamp the release writes, and `app.js` shows it as text.
- `style.css` gives the body a fixed grid (52px / 1fr / 1cm) with overflow hidden; the columns scroll.
- `sw.js` answers the site's own requests with `fetch(…, {cache: "no-cache"})`.
- The logo SVG carries explicit width and height, so no browser falls back to a default size.
- R8 in `docs/requirements.md` mentions the version.

Checks:
- In Chromium at 1600×900, 1280×720 and 1000×650 with a slide found:
  - the page height equals the window's;
  - the header is 52 px, the footer 38 px (1 cm) and the logo 36 px;
  - both side bars and the image scroll on their own.
- The page's own style.css and app.js now come through the service worker.
- The world check passes with 0 blocking findings.

{"number":228,"title":"Page: new layout, Find Candidates on demand, plus fixes for red-displayed DAPI, numbering and marks","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01NLfVm5WfzHBRRyA4oMF5jh?thread=cmsg_01NLfVm5WfzHBRRyA4oMF5jhKUmZ1vDWkaHNc4R6fwWVq9)_

Before:
- Some slides failed to load, on the page and in the lab, with "DAPI detected on a green/red channel".
- On the page, candidate numbers changed with every filter change.
- "remove" dropped a NoR from the list, and a reload forgot the marks.
- Nothing moved while Python loaded or a finder ran.
- Unticking "measuring lines" did nothing.
- The page ran the finder as soon as an image loaded. Everything was stacked in one column: controls on the left, the image, then the list and the summary further down.

After:
- Every fetched slide loads: 32 of 32, where 4 "Up Middle" slides failed before.
- Each candidate keeps one number, top to bottom, for the whole detection. A rejected one shows its number plus its letter, e.g. "12D".
- A removed NoR stays in the list, greyed out, with a "restore" button, and is left out of the totals.
- Stars and removals are saved in the browser per file name and finder.
- A spinner and an elapsed-time counter show while the page loads and while a finder runs.
- Unticking "measuring lines" hides them.
- The page is laid out in these parts:
  - **Header:** the logo, the title and a remembered dark/light switch. The logo is the three Sagol School marks in red, green and blue.
  - **Left bar:**
    - the image box: load, file name, and one checkbox per colour layer, with blue off at first;
    - the candidates finder: the algorithm, its main settings, a collapsed Advanced box with every setting, and a Find Candidates button;
    - the filters.
  - **Main area:** a toolbar (zoom, overlay options, and a big button that switches between the image and the individual items) over the two views.
  - **Right bar:** the summary.
  - **Status bar:** the image name, the candidate and finalist counts, and the time each step took.
- Loading an image no longer runs the finder. Find Candidates shines until it is pressed, and again whenever the finder or its settings change.

Why the slides failed: in the R,G,B files DAPI is displayed red, and the loader took the red-displayed channel to be Nav1.6.

How:
- `naive_nor.load` picks channels by role, as `data/README.md` prescribes. Caspr is the green-displayed channel, DAPI is whichever of the other two has larger blobs, and Nav1.6 is the rest. Slides that loaded before get the same channels. This also fixes the one file where the README says the blob test failed.
- The page numbers candidates once per detection.
- Marks are keyed by the candidate's rounded position under `nor-marks-v1:<file>|<finder>`.
- Each finder function declares its main settings in a `MAIN` tuple. `interactive.describe(finder)` gives the page a finder's filters and settings before it runs.
- `web/logo.svg` is traced from the logo Ariel supplied (`web/logo_source.png`) by `web/logo_trace.py`, which uses potracer. The insides of the marks are transparent, with no white fill.
- R8 in `docs/requirements.md` gains the new points.

Checks:
- `tests/test_load_channels.py` fails on main (4 slides) and passes here.
- `tests/test_interactive.py` passes, with the same 247 passes on the reference slide. Its new main-settings test fails without the `MAIN` declarations.
- In Chromium, on the old fixes:
  - 0 numbers moved across a filter change;
  - a remove and a star survived a reload;
  - the spinner showed during loading and finding;
  - lines, labels and rejected candidates each hide when unticked.
- In Chromium, on the new layout:
  - the button shines after a load and after a finder change, and not after a run;
  - main and Advanced settings stay in sync;

{"number":225,"title":"NoR Finder in the browser: detect once, filter live, served from GitHub Pages","body":"<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"missingbulb"} -->
_Requested by **Ariel** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01NLfVm5WfzHBRRyA4oMF5jh?thread=cmsg_01NLfVm5WfzHBRRyA4oMF5jhKUmZ1vDWkaHNc4R6fwWVq9)_

Before: the NoR finders ran only as Python scripts, and every change to a filter threshold meant re-running the finder and re-rendering the review PNGs.

After: a web page with no backend. You open a slide and it runs a finder once, taking about 15 s. After that every filter is a live dial, and each dial redraws the outlines, the cropped list of passing NoRs and the measurement summary in 20–50 ms. The detection settings are dials too, and the page warns that they re-run the finder. A ★ keeps a candidate in the list whatever the filters say. Filter settings are remembered in the browser, and "Restore filter defaults" puts back ours. Pyodide and the other third-party files are cached for 30 days. All five finders are offered, with traffic light as the default. The blue mask is only a filter (N) on the page.

The page runs the repo's own `detection/` and `src/` Python in the browser, unchanged. So a finder improvement, or a new check in `nor3.CHECKS`, reaches the page with no page change.

How: `detection/interactive.py` keeps one image's candidates and re-runs the checks, the nucleus rule and one-pixel-per-NoR on their stored measurements. `web/` runs it under Pyodide in a module worker, with a service worker that caches the third-party files. The page is deployed through the canon `github-pages` pack: it is declared and vendored with the install runner, `.github/site.config` names the published paths, and the pack's vendored deploy workflow does the upload.

Checks:
- `python3 tests/test_interactive.py` passes locally. At our settings the page passes exactly what the lab passes: `tl_post` with 247 passes, and rf's own 265. Turning a filter off frees exactly what it alone rejected. Every parameter a check reads is a control.
- The same flows were driven in headless Chromium: the first load, a filter change, reloading with saved settings, restore, a keeper, and switching to rf.
- The world and work sweeps are clean.

The two repository settings Pages needs are in #226.

Diff breadth: besides `web/` and `detection/interactive.py`, this touches `.claudinite/` and `.github/`. That is the pack adoption itself, and it is the pack's layout rather than something this change chose.

1	---
2	name: image-algorithm-development
3	description: State-by-state procedure for developing an image detection, segmentation or reading algorithm with an owner validating - which of the inputs, the approved render, the answer key and the grader exists yet, what to build next, what to ask and when to stop. Use when starting, resuming or iterating on any such algorithm, from microscope channels to phone photos.
4	metadata:
5	  body: workflow
6	  usage:
7	    expect: judgment
8	---
9	
10	# Developing an image detection, segmentation or reading algorithm
11	
12	research-project's `RULES.md` holds the standing rules - ground truth is annotated and never
13	invented, every change is shown as a picture, no overfitting to the learning set, numbered
14	iteration notes. This skill is the procedure they run inside: which state the project is in,
15	what to do there, and when to leave it. Examples come in pairs, **microscopy** (fluorescence
16	channels, cells and nodes, µm/px from metadata) and **phone photo** (books, receipts, labels at
17	everyday scale, EXIF and perspective); the method is the same and the examples are only examples.
18	
19	The work is three nested loops. The **outer loop** is the owner judging a render and answering
20	one question. The **inner loop** is you scoring a version against the answer key and keeping or
21	dropping it, with no owner. The **innermost loop** is build-until-working: run a change on one
22	sample and fix it until the stage emits the artefact it should (a mask, crops, numbers), before
23	it is scored. The states below build the loops from the outside in, because each loop needs the
24	artifact of the one outside it.
25	
26	## Ask at the start - one message, before any research
27	
28	1. **Which invariances the result must hold**: rotation, flip, scale (near vs far, one objective
29	   vs another), perspective, polarity, orientation, lighting, several objects per frame. Stated
30	   now, an invariance is a test in State 4; discovered later, it is a rebuild.
31	2. **Three to six diverse samples, each a different failure class**, not six of one condition -
32	   name the classes you want (microscopy: dense vs sparse, a dim channel, an out-of-focus tile, a
33	   stitched seam; phone: far, angled, glare, both polarities, upside down).
34	3. **Whether an answer key exists**; if not, whether a capable model may draft it, and whether
35	   the images may leave the machine or be committed at all.
36	4. **The tiers and what "good enough" means downstream** (a detection that lands the crop with a
37	   rough outline; a reading with a few wrong letters that still finds the catalogue entry).
38	5. **Where the code will run and the rough cost limit** (a workstation over a slide server; a
39	   phone or browser), so any library or engine survey is scoped once.
40	6. **Where the docs and the ledger live**, by the project's convention.
41	
42	Everything else in this skill you do without being asked. The answers are requirements; record
43	them with the ledger.
44	
45	## Find the state
46	
47	Check the gates in order; the first that fails is your state. Do not skip ahead - a scoring loop
48	without an approved answer key measures nothing, and a render nobody approved cannot be scored
49	against.
50	
51	| Gate | Test | If it fails |
52	|---|---|---|
53	| Inputs | one committed script fetches and verifies the inputs, and one loader returns pixels in a known frame with their scale | State 1 |
54	| Render | one render function exists and the owner has said they can judge results from it | State 2 |
55	| Answer key | labels the owner corrected in that render exist as data, with a held-out subset | State 3 |
56	| Grader | one command runs a version end to end and writes tiered scores, per-stage timings, the renders and the diff against the previous version | State 4, opening step |
57	| all pass | | State 4, iterate |
58	
59	Resuming a session: read the state off the repo (the loader, the render function, the key file,
60	the run command, and a committed state file saying where things stand and what is next), never
61	off memory of where things stood or off a project's side folder.
62	
63	## State 1 - no inputs you can reproduce
64	
65	Done when a fresh session runs one command and holds the same bytes, and every script calls the
66	one loader.
67	
68	- **Get the bytes onto disk first.** An image pasted into chat is not a file; search the session
69	  transcript for it before saying it did not arrive, and confirm the recovered file decodes to
70	  the expected dimensions.
71	- Fetch by committed script with a checksum. Store samples beside the answer key so the two
72	  travel together; large originals go outside git in a shared or cached location.
73	- **One loader, used everywhere, that normalises before anything reads a coordinate**: the frame
74	  (microscopy: channel order and per-channel offset; phone: EXIF orientation applied on decode,
75	  or every coordinate you report is sideways) and the scale, read from the input itself
76	  (microscopy: µm/px from the file's metadata, never a stated setting; phone: a reference object
77	  or the fixed working width, and say which).
78	- **Work on a working-resolution copy and cut detail from the original.** Fix the working size so
79	  every threshold means the same thing on every input, carry regions back to original
80	  coordinates, and crop fine detail (text, a node's outline) from full-resolution pixels. For
81	  very large images read regions (tiled or memory-mapped), develop on a representative crop and
82	  confirm on the full image; put a downscaled PNG in the chat, never the image itself.
83	- **Cache each expensive intermediate** that does not depend on what you tune (decoded channels,
84	  background, candidate crops, an engine's raw reading), keyed by input, stage and parameters;
85	  invalidate when the producing stage changes, and say in every summary line which stages ran
86	  cached.
87	- A library step that surprises you (chained operations that clobber each other, a channel count
88	  that changes on output) is materialised between steps and checked for shape, and goes in the
89	  ledger.
90	
91	No owner question here: choose defaults and state them.
92	
93	## State 2 - no approved render
94	
95	Done when the owner says, of one sample, that they can judge the result from it, and the render
96	is one function every later version calls. Build it on one sample, before any algorithm work:
97	the owner knows what the right output looks like, and this render is the interface they judge
98	through.
99	
100	- **Overlay on the input**, mask or thin semi-transparent outline (research-project §1 owns style
101	  and colour), every item numbered in reading order and colour-coded by status (found / at the
102	  frame edge / rejected, each reject tagged with the rule that removed it).
103	- **Draw the geometry you actually compute**, not a simplification: a fitted ellipse as an
104	  ellipse, a tilted line tilted, a perspective quadrilateral as the trapezoid it is. An
105	  axis-aligned box over a tilted object hides the alignment assumption from you and the owner
106	  until they point it out.
107	- **A per-item sheet**: each object as the next stage sees it (the crop after warp, inversion or
108	  flattening; the node crop with its channel profiles) with that stage's output beside it. A
109	  cut-off crop or a biased reader becomes visible here and nowhere else. Add a zoom of a dense
110	  region; the full overlay alone is too small to judge.
111	- **A machine-readable result** (`result.json`) with every intermediate decision and per-stage
112	  timings, so "why did #7 fail" is answered without a re-run.
113	- **One CLI**: `tool <image> [out-dir]` writes overlay, sheet and result and prints one summary
114	  line (`18/21 found · segment 1.2 s · classify 0.4 s · cached: none`).
115	- Check the render itself before showing it - label overlap, numbering matching the JSON, text
116	  anchoring - because a wrong overlay wastes a round.
117	
118	Ask the owner one question with the render: "Can you tell from this which objects are right and
119	which are wrong - and what is missing to decide?" Iterate on the format until the answer is yes,
120	then freeze it.
121	
122	**The frozen render is an API with the owner.** Its colours, outlines, numbering, panels and list
123	columns change only when the owner asks; propose a change with a before/after on the same sample
124	and wait, and until then every version renders the approved way, even when a new filter or
125	output needs a place in it. The committed render function is the only definition of the format:
126	render every version through it, never from a note describing the style, because notes go stale
127	when the owner changes the format. The one change that needs no asking: when the owner corrects a
128	geometric assumption, the next render draws the corrected geometry.
129	
130	## Many objects in one image - decide on divide and conquer
131	
132	When the task detects many objects per image, settle this before State 3, because it decides
133	what the answer key and the inner loop work on. If the objects are discrete and do not affect one
134	another visually, pursue divide and conquer: propose candidate sub-images (crops, each around one
135	object with a margin) with a cheap generic step, and develop, label and score the detector on
136	those. Crops are faster to label, cheaper to iterate on, and easy to review as contact sheets.
137	
138	- Show the owner (or have a capable model pre-screen, then the owner confirm) a sheet of a few
139	  sub-images, and ask two questions: "Is each crop one independent object of the kind we want?"
140	  and "Do you see visual interaction between neighbours - touching, overlapping, shared signal,
141	  one object's glow or shadow on the next?" (microscopy: stain bleed, a bright neighbour's halo;
142	  phone: one spine's shadow on the next, a reflection).
143	- **No interaction:** work on sub-images from here on, with the crop step as its own scored
144	  stage, since an object never proposed is lost for good.
145	- **Interaction:** a tight crop throws away information. Try a wider crop that includes the
146	  neighbours as context while labelling only the centre object, and show the owner that sheet.
147	  If wider crops still lose what matters, work on the whole image.
148	
149	Record the decision and its reason in the ledger.
150	
151	## State 3 - no answer key
152	
153	Done when a few inputs carry labels the owner verified in the State 2 render, stored as data
154	beside the samples, with a few inputs held out of tuning. Get it before tuning anything, or every
155	improvement is an opinion. Take the first branch that applies:
156	
157	1. **The owner has annotations** - parse and register them (research-project §2 owns parsing,
158	   regeneration and self-checks).
159	2. **No annotations** - draft them with a capable model: give it the inputs and the owner's
160	   stated requirements, run it on the crops the pipeline sees where the whole image is too small
161	   for it, and **show the draft to the owner before using it**, in the State 2 render and as a
162	   table beside your own reading, saying where it is weak. Where model and you agree, trust;
163	   where you disagree, ask. Only the corrected set is ground truth. Leave this branch when the
164	   owner corrects more than they keep.
165	3. **No model drafts something the owner can fix quickly** - you label from full-resolution
166	   crops, every entry marked unconfirmed, and ask only about the uncertain ones.
167	4. **None of these** - the owner labels a few inputs by hand, with the render tool ready for
168	   them; State 4 waits until it exists.
169	
170	**The key's shape** - one file, with an `_about` field explaining every other field:
171	
172	- Per item: position or outline, the expected reading or class, and `confirmed` true or false.
173	  Unconfirmed is your reading, not yet checked; never promote it silently.
174	- `"?"` marks an unknowable item (illegible, cut off, out of focus, physically hidden) - kept,
175	  never graded, never spent an iteration on.
176	- `notes` says *why* an item is hard ("upside down", "on the tile seam", "two cells touching");
177	  these are the known-gap list and the classes for the next sample request.
178	- **Partial keys are fine.** Key the 35 items you know of 150, with a scope field (a region, a
179	  shelf, a tile) so the grader pairs only inside it and does not read the unkeyed rest as misses.
180	- **Record occlusion and grade only what is visible** (the shelf lip hides every author; the
181	  coverslip edge clips a row of nodes). A metric that penalises content not in the pixels teaches
182	  nothing.
183	- **Reuse answers across overlapping inputs.** When one sample shows objects other samples show
184	  under a different angle, distance or exposure, key it from them - a scale and angle test for
185	  free. Look for the overlap yourself.
186	
187	**Asking about uncertain entries**: one lettered list (A-J, about ten at a time), each with the
188	item number and your best reading, and one image with the same letters on the crops. The owner
189	answers `A - check`, `E - <correction>`, `G - can't tell either`. List the confident entries in
190	one line so they can object without being asked item by item; anything unanswered stays
191	unconfirmed. Expect corrections no metric produces ("these two are not objects", "nothing
192	printed there", "hidden") and encode each as a key field, never a code special-case.
193	
194	Until the owner has answered, every count you report is a proxy - say so beside the number.
195	
196	## State 4 - the answer key exists: run the inner loop
197	
198	Opening step, if the Grader gate failed: write the one command (`score [--verbose] [--only
199	<sample>] [--cache]`) that runs every sample and writes, per version into its own folder: the
200	tiered score, reject counts per reason, which rule removed each missed real object, per-stage
201	timings, the renders, and the objects gained and lost against the previous version.
202	
203	- **Tiers, not one score**: `full` / `partial` / `missed` with thresholds that mean something
204	  downstream (an outline within the tolerance the measurement needs; a reading close enough to
205	  find the entry). Tiers tell the owner where to look; a mean IoU does not. Precision, recall and
206	  F1 are the totals under them.
207	- **Greedy pairing** of key items to detections: a distance for every pair, closest first, each
208	  side used once, constrained by the scope field. Robust to extras, misses and reordering.
209	- **Grade on what matters downstream**: strip what the consumer ignores before comparing
210	  (punctuation and word order; an outline's sub-pixel wobble), or that noise swamps the signal.
211	- **Grade every stage** with its own tiers (proposal / classification / measurement;
212	  segmentation / reading / matching): a gain in one stage can hurt the next.
213	- **Beat the noise.** Re-run the baseline in the same session before comparing; judge on totals
214	  over all samples, never one item or one sample; on a few dozen graded items a gain of one or
215	  two is noise - find a change that moves five, or get more samples. Mark every number cached,
216	  fresh or synthetic.
217	- **Decide keep or drop by a stated rule, not by eye.** Compare a variant with the current version
218	  by a paired bootstrap over the keyed items (resample items, score both on each draw) and read
219	  P(variant better): keep at ≥ 0.8, drop at ≤ 0.2, and in between call it no evidence and keep
220	  the simpler option or the incumbent. Print the verdict beside the tp/fp counts, one line per
221	  variant, from one command.
222	- **Naive first.** Before adding a stage, score the simplest whole-image approach; add the stage
223	  only when the naive run fails on the metric, and cite that run in the ledger.
224	
225	Each iteration:
226	
227	1. **Score**, reading `--verbose` (one line per item: tier, expected, got, outcome) and the
228	   gained/lost sheets rather than full renders - that keeps an iteration cheap in tokens.
229	2. **Diagnose the largest error class and locate its stage**: *generation* (never proposed whole
230	   - parts not separated, merged with a neighbour, cut off by the crop) or *filtering* (a good
231	   candidate rejected or misread). Check the earlier stage before tuning the later one: most
232	   "reader" or "classifier" failures are crop failures. A reject reason meaning "the candidate
233	   was malformed" measures the generator, not the filter; when it dominates, rebuild the
234	   generator - tuning the filter that catches it only hides the fault.
235	3. **Change one thing, naming the mechanism** ("the band line sits mid-object because it is
236	   fitted to edge density, not each object's own extent"), in a new version. For a generator
237	   rebuild, first write how you would explain finding the object to a child, in steps concrete
238	   enough to draw, and implement that; if it fails, write a completely different explanation
239	   rather than patch the old one.
240	4. **Build until working** on the sample render before scoring.
241	5. **Keep or drop on the score**, reviewing the gained and lost objects, and write the iteration
242	   note (research-project §5). Record the attempt in the ledger whether kept or dropped.
243	   **Land every change as a switch** in the version's parameters, the old behaviour one value
244	   away, and test each switch alone against the current version, owner-pitched ideas included.
245	   When a change is several ideas at once (a new generator with a new shape rule and a new
246	   pairing rule), ablate each part; a pitched part that loses on the data is turned off and
247	   reported with its numbers, not quietly kept or removed.
248	
249	Cheap moves between iterations:
250	
251	- **Rescue false negatives** - pick a few clear real objects that were lost, find the rule that
252	  killed each, adjust that rule, rescore. Repeat while it keeps paying.
253	- **Work the lost list after a new version.** Take the objects the previous version passed and
254	  this one does not, rank them (keyed-real first, then the largest reject class among the rest),
255	  look at a paired sheet (old outline beside new) for the largest class, write the fix as
256	  pseudocode that names the mechanism, implement it as a switch, and ablate it.
257	- **Measure each filter alone** - how many it rejects on its own and how many it is the *only*
258	  reason for. Order the strictest first; a filter that is almost never the only reason is
259	  redundant - drop it, or show the owner the objects only it rejects.
260	- **Run a capable model on the same items as a reference point**, not only as a key source: its
261	  tiers beside yours say whether the gap is the pipeline or the pixels.
262	
263	**Every change passes the assumption test before it is kept.** Every constant needs a sentence
264	saying what it is relative to and where it came from; if the sentence is "it worked on sample 1",
265	it is a bug that has not failed yet.
266	
267	| Legitimate | Illegitimate |
268	|---|---|
269	| Sizes and cut-offs relative to what the image measures for itself: µm from metadata or multiples of the median object size; noise multiples, fractions of local intensity or an Otsu split, the dominant edge angle | Absolute pixel counts, distances or intensities that happen to work on the samples |
270	| Quantities that scale with resolution (halve a gradient threshold when the working width doubles) | Re-tuning the same constant by hand after every resolution change |
271	| Domain priors from how the object is made, cited in the code (a node's marker arrangement from the literature; text runs along a spine and is the minority of its pixels) | Priors true of your samples only (every cell in focus; every book upright and dark-on-light) |
272	| Multi-hypothesis when a measured statistic is ambiguous (near 50/50 polarity → process both ways, keep the better) | One hypothesis chosen by a bar set to pass the sample |
273	| A second, looser pass triggered by a measured anomaly (a segment wider than 1.8× the median is re-searched for a merge) | Lowering the global threshold until the sample passes |
274	| Downstream tolerance for what the pixels cannot resolve (two glyphs identical at ten pixels; two markers inside one point-spread) | Endless crop tweaking for detail that is not in the pixels |
275	
276	A change that only scores better with an illegitimate constant is dropped (research-project §4);
277	when samples are few, prefer the change with a physical explanation over the better score.
278	
279	**Every kept version passes the invariance stress test**, one transform per invariance the owner
280	stated. Never assume the object is aligned to the pixel grid. Run the version on transformed
281	copies of an input and map the detections back: rotations including non-right angles (15°, 30°,
282	45°) and flips for any image; shear, anisotropic scaling and perspective skew for anything a
283	camera or microscope can project; polarity and lighting where stated. Detections must match the
284	untransformed run within explicit bounds per transform, in a committed executable test (this
285	repo's `tests/test_invariance.py` is one). The test needs no key - it checks the algorithm against
286	itself, so a detector that finds nothing passes and it never replaces the score - and a synthetic
287	transform resamples twice, so it is pessimistic; say so. Recall that drops under a transform is an
288	orientation or shape assumption: find it and remove it, as with an illegitimate constant. Unit
289	tests of pure-pixel stages may use drawn synthetic inputs; the score and invariance harnesses run
290	on real images (research-project §3).
291	
292	**Stuck** - no error class you can name, or every fix trades one error for another: research the
293	*object*, not the code - how it is made, printed or stained, its dimensions and arrangement, what
294	published methods and the engine's docs say - and turn that into legitimate assumptions before
295	trying another parameter.
296	
297	**Stop iterating after two consecutive iterations without a gain beyond noise**, or when every
298	remaining miss is a `notes` class that needs the owner or a new direction, and go to the owner.
299	
300	## The ledger - every direction tried, and why it won or lost
301	
302	Keep one ledger file where the owner said docs go, appended every time an algorithmic direction,
303	a performance attempt, a library gotcha or an owner-pitched idea is tried or set aside. It is
304	what lets a later session, or a changed problem, reuse an idea instead of rediscovering it, so
305	each entry is specific enough to act on without the code:
306	
307	- **The idea**, in one line, and its **source** (your diagnosis, the literature, or the owner).
308	- **The mechanism**: what it computes, with its parameters, in scale-free terms.
309	- **The result**: the tier deltas per sample, and what it fixed.
310	- **Where it failed**: the error class or image condition that beat it, with object numbers or a
311	  sheet path.
312	- **When to revisit**: the change in the problem, data or constraints that would make it worth
313	  trying again.
314	
315	Before starting a new direction, search the ledger for it and for its failure conditions. An
316	owner-pitched idea gets an entry even when you did not try it, stating why. The dated scoring
317	table, per sample per version, lives in the same place; every entry cites its rows.
318	
319	## Between stretches - make the cycle cheaper
320	
321	Every iteration of both loops pays in time, tokens, CPU and RAM. Quality comes first; a
322	performance pass is its own step, after a stretch of quality work and never while the owner waits
323	on a result - unless a grader run has crept past what a feedback round can tolerate, in which
324	case say so and spend one cycle on it. The per-stage timings in every summary line are the early
325	warning.
326	
327	- Profile the current version, fix the top hotspot, and prove the output identical by hashing
328	  both; a pass that changes a result is a quality change and is scored as one. Report the time
329	  before and after, and log the attempt in the ledger, including one that was reverted. Hash the
330	  outputs themselves (positions, verdicts, segment pixels), not a summary count. Time the
331	  minimum of a few runs: run-to-run noise on a shared machine can reach ±15%, so a small gain is
332	  re-checked before it is claimed. A lower-precision type is a classic trap: faster, but it
333	  changes ties, so the hash catches it.
334	- Restore the token budget the same way: if you have been reading full renders, fix the run
335	  command's summary until the score and the gained/lost sheets are enough.
336	- **Deployment is not quality work**: memory limits, instance sizes, job APIs and device ports are
337	  their own tasks with their own measurements, and a cost comparison of alternatives (per item,
338	  dated list prices, what leaves the machine) is a table in the docs, not a round's report.
339	
340	## Going to the owner
341	
342	Go when one of these holds; otherwise keep running the inner loop alone:
343	
344	- the render (State 2) or the answer key (State 3) needs approval, or a stage's overlay is ready
345	  - stop after each stage's overlay, not after the whole pipeline
346	- two iterations without a gain beyond noise
347	- a fix would add a criterion for what the object *is* - only the owner adds domain rules
348	- a filter's threshold is in doubt - show the objects only that filter rejects
349	- the objects look separable: approve sample sub-images and say whether neighbours interact
350	- a large sample would take long to key: ask whether to key it or keep it as a readability-only
351	  test, rather than guess
352	- a version is about to be called final or run on new inputs
353	
354	**How to ask:** one checkpoint: one image with numbered overlays, one lettered list of the
355	uncertain items, one before/after table, one status line (`all: 23 full, 26 partial, 37 missed ·
356	sample6 weakest`), and "what I need from you" as a numbered list at the end. One concrete
357	question per render ("objects 4, 9 and 12 are rejected only by the elongation filter - are they
358	real?"); batch rather than interrupt per finding.
359	
360	**How to report at each exit:** the numbers before and after, what changed, and each remaining
361	failure with its class and whether it needs the owner (unknowable, hidden, a new sample class) or
362	a new direction. That last part is what earns the next round of useful feedback instead of a
363	repeat of the last one.
364	
365	**How to take the answer:** the owner tends to answer with a rule ("anything touching the edge is
366	not real") rather than with labels. Encode each rule as a check in the pipeline, a key field or an
367	invariance test, so the inner loop runs on it without the owner, then return to State 4. Only the
368	owner supplies object identity, physical facts of the scene (the trapezoid, the hidden author,
369	the stain that bleeds), key corrections, new sample classes and direction; the method - real
370	geometry, naive first, uncertain items only, show before using - is this skill's and should not
371	need saying twice.
372	
373	## Where the two disciplines differ
374	
375	| | Microscopy | Phone photo of everyday objects |
376	|---|---|---|
377	| Scale and frame | µm/px and channel order from the file's metadata; z and focus per tile; stitched-tile seams | EXIF orientation; no absolute scale without a reference object; perspective, so parallel edges converge |
378	| Typical invariances | rotation and flip; intensity scale across exposures; channel gain | rotation and perspective; distance; lighting and glare; polarity; upside-down objects |
379	| Typical failure classes | stain bleed between channels, out-of-focus regions, touching cells, dim signal against autofluorescence, edge clipping | a crop cutting an item, two items in one crop, glare, text below the pixels, illustrated or stylised surfaces |
380	| A ground-truth label | a position or outline per object with real / not real / unsure, registered to the loader's frame | a per-item reading or class with `confirmed`, `"?"` for unknowable, a scope field, occlusion flags |
381
