---
name: image-algorithm-development
description: State-by-state procedure for developing an image detection, segmentation or reading algorithm with an owner validating - which of the inputs, the approved render, the answer key and the grader exists yet, what to build next, what to ask and when to stop. Use when starting, resuming or iterating on any such algorithm, from microscope channels to phone photos.
metadata:
  body: workflow
  usage:
    expect: judgment
---

# Developing an image detection, segmentation or reading algorithm

research-project's `RULES.md` holds the standing rules - ground truth is annotated and never
invented, every change is shown as a picture, no overfitting to the learning set, numbered
iteration notes. This skill is the procedure they run inside: which state the project is in,
what to do there, and when to leave it. Examples come in pairs, **microscopy** (fluorescence
channels, cells and nodes, µm/px from metadata) and **phone photo** (books, receipts, labels at
everyday scale, EXIF and perspective); the method is the same and the examples are only examples.

The work is three nested loops. The **outer loop** is the owner judging a render and answering
one question. The **inner loop** is you scoring a version against the answer key and keeping or
dropping it, with no owner. The **innermost loop** is build-until-working: run a change on one
sample and fix it until the stage emits the artefact it should (a mask, crops, numbers), before
it is scored. The states below build the loops from the outside in, because each loop needs the
artifact of the one outside it.

## Ask at the start - one message, before any research

1. **Which invariances the result must hold**: rotation, flip, scale (near vs far, one objective
   vs another), perspective, polarity, orientation, lighting, several objects per frame. Stated
   now, an invariance is a test in State 4; discovered later, it is a rebuild.
2. **Three to six diverse samples, each a different failure class**, not six of one condition -
   name the classes you want (microscopy: dense vs sparse, a dim channel, an out-of-focus tile, a
   stitched seam; phone: far, angled, glare, both polarities, upside down).
3. **Whether an answer key exists**; if not, whether a capable model may draft it, and whether
   the images may leave the machine or be committed at all.
4. **The tiers and what "good enough" means downstream** (a detection that lands the crop with a
   rough outline; a reading with a few wrong letters that still finds the catalogue entry).
5. **Where the code will run and the rough cost limit** (a workstation over a slide server; a
   phone or browser), so any library or engine survey is scoped once.
6. **Where the docs and the ledger live**, by the project's convention.

Everything else in this skill you do without being asked. The answers are requirements; record
them with the ledger.

## Find the state

Check the gates in order; the first that fails is your state. Do not skip ahead - a scoring loop
without an approved answer key measures nothing, and a render nobody approved cannot be scored
against.

| Gate | Test | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| Inputs | one committed script fetches and verifies the inputs, and one loader returns pixels in a known frame with their scale | State 1 |
| Render | one render function exists and the owner has said they can judge results from it | State 2 |
| Answer key | labels the owner corrected in that render exist as data, with a held-out subset | State 3 |
| Grader | one command runs a version end to end and writes tiered scores, per-stage timings, the renders and the diff against the previous version | State 4, opening step |
| all pass | | State 4, iterate |

Resuming a session: read the state off the repo (the loader, the render function, the key file,
the run command, and a committed state file saying where things stand and what is next), never
off memory of where things stood or off a project's side folder.

## State 1 - no inputs you can reproduce

Done when a fresh session runs one command and holds the same bytes, and every script calls the
one loader.

- **Get the bytes onto disk first.** An image pasted into chat is not a file; search the session
  transcript for it before saying it did not arrive, and confirm the recovered file decodes to
  the expected dimensions.
- Fetch by committed script with a checksum. Store samples beside the answer key so the two
  travel together; large originals go outside git in a shared or cached location.
- **One loader, used everywhere, that normalises before anything reads a coordinate**: the frame
  (microscopy: channel order and per-channel offset; phone: EXIF orientation applied on decode,
  or every coordinate you report is sideways) and the scale, read from the input itself
  (microscopy: µm/px from the file's metadata, never a stated setting; phone: a reference object
  or the fixed working width, and say which).
- **Work on a working-resolution copy and cut detail from the original.** Fix the working size so
  every threshold means the same thing on every input, carry regions back to original
  coordinates, and crop fine detail (text, a node's outline) from full-resolution pixels. For
  very large images read regions (tiled or memory-mapped), develop on a representative crop and
  confirm on the full image; put a downscaled PNG in the chat, never the image itself.
- **Cache each expensive intermediate** that does not depend on what you tune (decoded channels,
  background, candidate crops, an engine's raw reading), keyed by input, stage and parameters;
  invalidate when the producing stage changes, and say in every summary line which stages ran
  cached.
- A library step that surprises you (chained operations that clobber each other, a channel count
  that changes on output) is materialised between steps and checked for shape, and goes in the
  ledger.

No owner question here: choose defaults and state them.

## State 2 - no approved render

Done when the owner says, of one sample, that they can judge the result from it, and the render
is one function every later version calls. Build it on one sample, before any algorithm work:
the owner knows what the right output looks like, and this render is the interface they judge
through.

- **Overlay on the input**, mask or thin semi-transparent outline (research-project §1 owns style
  and colour), every item numbered in reading order and colour-coded by status (found / at the
  frame edge / rejected, each reject tagged with the rule that removed it).
- **Draw the geometry you actually compute**, not a simplification: a fitted ellipse as an
  ellipse, a tilted line tilted, a perspective quadrilateral as the trapezoid it is. An
  axis-aligned box over a tilted object hides the alignment assumption from you and the owner
  until they point it out.
- **A per-item sheet**: each object as the next stage sees it (the crop after warp, inversion or
  flattening; the node crop with its channel profiles) with that stage's output beside it. A
  cut-off crop or a biased reader becomes visible here and nowhere else. Add a zoom of a dense
  region; the full overlay alone is too small to judge.
- **A machine-readable result** (`result.json`) with every intermediate decision and per-stage
  timings, so "why did #7 fail" is answered without a re-run.
- **One CLI**: `tool <image> [out-dir]` writes overlay, sheet and result and prints one summary
  line (`18/21 found · segment 1.2 s · classify 0.4 s · cached: none`).
- Check the render itself before showing it - label overlap, numbering matching the JSON, text
  anchoring - because a wrong overlay wastes a round.

Ask the owner one question with the render: "Can you tell from this which objects are right and
which are wrong - and what is missing to decide?" Iterate on the format until the answer is yes,
then freeze it.

**The frozen render is an API with the owner.** Its colours, outlines, numbering, panels and list
columns change only when the owner asks; propose a change with a before/after on the same sample
and wait, and until then every version renders the approved way, even when a new filter or
output needs a place in it. The committed render function is the only definition of the format:
render every version through it, never from a note describing the style, because notes go stale
when the owner changes the format. The one change that needs no asking: when the owner corrects a
geometric assumption, the next render draws the corrected geometry.

## Many objects in one image - decide on divide and conquer

When the task detects many objects per image, settle this before State 3, because it decides
what the answer key and the inner loop work on. If the objects are discrete and do not affect one
another visually, pursue divide and conquer: propose candidate sub-images (crops, each around one
object with a margin) with a cheap generic step, and develop, label and score the detector on
those. Crops are faster to label, cheaper to iterate on, and easy to review as contact sheets.

- Show the owner (or have a capable model pre-screen, then the owner confirm) a sheet of a few
  sub-images, and ask two questions: "Is each crop one independent object of the kind we want?"
  and "Do you see visual interaction between neighbours - touching, overlapping, shared signal,
  one object's glow or shadow on the next?" (microscopy: stain bleed, a bright neighbour's halo;
  phone: one spine's shadow on the next, a reflection).
- **No interaction:** work on sub-images from here on, with the crop step as its own scored
  stage, since an object never proposed is lost for good.
- **Interaction:** a tight crop throws away information. Try a wider crop that includes the
  neighbours as context while labelling only the centre object, and show the owner that sheet.
  If wider crops still lose what matters, work on the whole image.

Record the decision and its reason in the ledger.

## State 3 - no answer key

Done when a few inputs carry labels the owner verified in the State 2 render, stored as data
beside the samples, with a few inputs held out of tuning. Get it before tuning anything, or every
improvement is an opinion. Take the first branch that applies:

1. **The owner has annotations** - parse and register them (research-project §2 owns parsing,
   regeneration and self-checks).
2. **No annotations** - draft them with a capable model: give it the inputs and the owner's
   stated requirements, run it on the crops the pipeline sees where the whole image is too small
   for it, and **show the draft to the owner before using it**, in the State 2 render and as a
   table beside your own reading, saying where it is weak. Where model and you agree, trust;
   where you disagree, ask. Only the corrected set is ground truth. Leave this branch when the
   owner corrects more than they keep.
3. **No model drafts something the owner can fix quickly** - you label from full-resolution
   crops, every entry marked unconfirmed, and ask only about the uncertain ones.
4. **None of these** - the owner labels a few inputs by hand, with the render tool ready for
   them; State 4 waits until it exists.

**The key's shape** - one file, with an `_about` field explaining every other field:

- Per item: position or outline, the expected reading or class, and `confirmed` true or false.
  Unconfirmed is your reading, not yet checked; never promote it silently.
- `"?"` marks an unknowable item (illegible, cut off, out of focus, physically hidden) - kept,
  never graded, never spent an iteration on.
- `notes` says *why* an item is hard ("upside down", "on the tile seam", "two cells touching");
  these are the known-gap list and the classes for the next sample request.
- **Partial keys are fine.** Key the 35 items you know of 150, with a scope field (a region, a
  shelf, a tile) so the grader pairs only inside it and does not read the unkeyed rest as misses.
- **Record occlusion and grade only what is visible** (the shelf lip hides every author; the
  coverslip edge clips a row of nodes). A metric that penalises content not in the pixels teaches
  nothing.
- **Reuse answers across overlapping inputs.** When one sample shows objects other samples show
  under a different angle, distance or exposure, key it from them - a scale and angle test for
  free. Look for the overlap yourself.

**Asking about uncertain entries**: one lettered list (A-J, about ten at a time), each with the
item number and your best reading, and one image with the same letters on the crops. The owner
answers `A - check`, `E - <correction>`, `G - can't tell either`. List the confident entries in
one line so they can object without being asked item by item; anything unanswered stays
unconfirmed. Expect corrections no metric produces ("these two are not objects", "nothing
printed there", "hidden") and encode each as a key field, never a code special-case.

Until the owner has answered, every count you report is a proxy - say so beside the number.

## State 4 - the answer key exists: run the inner loop

Opening step, if the Grader gate failed: write the one command (`score [--verbose] [--only
<sample>] [--cache]`) that runs every sample and writes, per version into its own folder: the
tiered score, reject counts per reason, which rule removed each missed real object, per-stage
timings, the renders, and the objects gained and lost against the previous version.

- **Tiers, not one score**: `full` / `partial` / `missed` with thresholds that mean something
  downstream (an outline within the tolerance the measurement needs; a reading close enough to
  find the entry). Tiers tell the owner where to look; a mean IoU does not. Precision, recall and
  F1 are the totals under them.
- **Greedy pairing** of key items to detections: a distance for every pair, closest first, each
  side used once, constrained by the scope field. Robust to extras, misses and reordering.
- **Grade on what matters downstream**: strip what the consumer ignores before comparing
  (punctuation and word order; an outline's sub-pixel wobble), or that noise swamps the signal.
- **Grade every stage** with its own tiers (proposal / classification / measurement;
  segmentation / reading / matching): a gain in one stage can hurt the next.
- **Beat the noise.** Re-run the baseline in the same session before comparing; judge on totals
  over all samples, never one item or one sample; on a few dozen graded items a gain of one or
  two is noise - find a change that moves five, or get more samples. Mark every number cached,
  fresh or synthetic.
- **Decide keep or drop by a stated rule, not by eye.** Compare a variant with the current version
  by a paired bootstrap over the keyed items (resample items, score both on each draw) and read
  P(variant better): keep at ≥ 0.8, drop at ≤ 0.2, and in between call it no evidence and keep
  the simpler option or the incumbent. Print the verdict beside the tp/fp counts, one line per
  variant, from one command.
- **Naive first.** Before adding a stage, score the simplest whole-image approach; add the stage
  only when the naive run fails on the metric, and cite that run in the ledger.

Each iteration:

1. **Score**, reading `--verbose` (one line per item: tier, expected, got, outcome) and the
   gained/lost sheets rather than full renders - that keeps an iteration cheap in tokens.
2. **Diagnose the largest error class and locate its stage**: *generation* (never proposed whole
   - parts not separated, merged with a neighbour, cut off by the crop) or *filtering* (a good
   candidate rejected or misread). Check the earlier stage before tuning the later one: most
   "reader" or "classifier" failures are crop failures. A reject reason meaning "the candidate
   was malformed" measures the generator, not the filter; when it dominates, rebuild the
   generator - tuning the filter that catches it only hides the fault.
3. **Change one thing, naming the mechanism** ("the band line sits mid-object because it is
   fitted to edge density, not each object's own extent"), in a new version. For a generator
   rebuild, first write how you would explain finding the object to a child, in steps concrete
   enough to draw, and implement that; if it fails, write a completely different explanation
   rather than patch the old one.
4. **Build until working** on the sample render before scoring.
5. **Keep or drop on the score**, reviewing the gained and lost objects, and write the iteration
   note (research-project §5). Record the attempt in the ledger whether kept or dropped.
   **Land every change as a switch** in the version's parameters, the old behaviour one value
   away, and test each switch alone against the current version, owner-pitched ideas included.
   When a change is several ideas at once (a new generator with a new shape rule and a new
   pairing rule), ablate each part; a pitched part that loses on the data is turned off and
   reported with its numbers, not quietly kept or removed.

Cheap moves between iterations:

- **Rescue false negatives** - pick a few clear real objects that were lost, find the rule that
  killed each, adjust that rule, rescore. Repeat while it keeps paying.
- **Work the lost list after a new version.** Take the objects the previous version passed and
  this one does not, rank them (keyed-real first, then the largest reject class among the rest),
  look at a paired sheet (old outline beside new) for the largest class, write the fix as
  pseudocode that names the mechanism, implement it as a switch, and ablate it.
- **Measure each filter alone** - how many it rejects on its own and how many it is the *only*
  reason for. Order the strictest first; a filter that is almost never the only reason is
  redundant - drop it, or show the owner the objects only it rejects.
- **Run a capable model on the same items as a reference point**, not only as a key source: its
  tiers beside yours say whether the gap is the pipeline or the pixels.

**Every change passes the assumption test before it is kept.** Every constant needs a sentence
saying what it is relative to and where it came from; if the sentence is "it worked on sample 1",
it is a bug that has not failed yet.

| Legitimate | Illegitimate |
|---|---|
| Sizes and cut-offs relative to what the image measures for itself: µm from metadata or multiples of the median object size; noise multiples, fractions of local intensity or an Otsu split, the dominant edge angle | Absolute pixel counts, distances or intensities that happen to work on the samples |
| Quantities that scale with resolution (halve a gradient threshold when the working width doubles) | Re-tuning the same constant by hand after every resolution change |
| Domain priors from how the object is made, cited in the code (a node's marker arrangement from the literature; text runs along a spine and is the minority of its pixels) | Priors true of your samples only (every cell in focus; every book upright and dark-on-light) |
| Multi-hypothesis when a measured statistic is ambiguous (near 50/50 polarity → process both ways, keep the better) | One hypothesis chosen by a bar set to pass the sample |
| A second, looser pass triggered by a measured anomaly (a segment wider than 1.8× the median is re-searched for a merge) | Lowering the global threshold until the sample passes |
| Downstream tolerance for what the pixels cannot resolve (two glyphs identical at ten pixels; two markers inside one point-spread) | Endless crop tweaking for detail that is not in the pixels |

A change that only scores better with an illegitimate constant is dropped (research-project §4);
when samples are few, prefer the change with a physical explanation over the better score.

**Every kept version passes the invariance stress test**, one transform per invariance the owner
stated. Never assume the object is aligned to the pixel grid. Run the version on transformed
copies of an input and map the detections back: rotations including non-right angles (15°, 30°,
45°) and flips for any image; shear, anisotropic scaling and perspective skew for anything a
camera or microscope can project; polarity and lighting where stated. Detections must match the
untransformed run within explicit bounds per transform, in a committed executable test (this
repo's `tests/test_invariance.py` is one). The test needs no key - it checks the algorithm against
itself, so a detector that finds nothing passes and it never replaces the score - and a synthetic
transform resamples twice, so it is pessimistic; say so. Recall that drops under a transform is an
orientation or shape assumption: find it and remove it, as with an illegitimate constant. Unit
tests of pure-pixel stages may use drawn synthetic inputs; the score and invariance harnesses run
on real images (research-project §3).

**Stuck** - no error class you can name, or every fix trades one error for another: research the
*object*, not the code - how it is made, printed or stained, its dimensions and arrangement, what
published methods and the engine's docs say - and turn that into legitimate assumptions before
trying another parameter.

**Stop iterating after two consecutive iterations without a gain beyond noise**, or when every
remaining miss is a `notes` class that needs the owner or a new direction, and go to the owner.

## The ledger - every direction tried, and why it won or lost

Keep one ledger file where the owner said docs go, appended every time an algorithmic direction,
a performance attempt, a library gotcha or an owner-pitched idea is tried or set aside. It is
what lets a later session, or a changed problem, reuse an idea instead of rediscovering it, so
each entry is specific enough to act on without the code:

- **The idea**, in one line, and its **source** (your diagnosis, the literature, or the owner).
- **The mechanism**: what it computes, with its parameters, in scale-free terms.
- **The result**: the tier deltas per sample, and what it fixed.
- **Where it failed**: the error class or image condition that beat it, with object numbers or a
  sheet path.
- **When to revisit**: the change in the problem, data or constraints that would make it worth
  trying again.

Before starting a new direction, search the ledger for it and for its failure conditions. An
owner-pitched idea gets an entry even when you did not try it, stating why. The dated scoring
table, per sample per version, lives in the same place; every entry cites its rows.

## Between stretches - make the cycle cheaper

Every iteration of both loops pays in time, tokens, CPU and RAM. Quality comes first; a
performance pass is its own step, after a stretch of quality work and never while the owner waits
on a result - unless a grader run has crept past what a feedback round can tolerate, in which
case say so and spend one cycle on it. The per-stage timings in every summary line are the early
warning.

- Profile the current version, fix the top hotspot, and prove the output identical by hashing
  both; a pass that changes a result is a quality change and is scored as one. Report the time
  before and after, and log the attempt in the ledger, including one that was reverted. Hash the
  outputs themselves (positions, verdicts, segment pixels), not a summary count. Time the
  minimum of a few runs: run-to-run noise on a shared machine can reach ±15%, so a small gain is
  re-checked before it is claimed. A lower-precision type is a classic trap: faster, but it
  changes ties, so the hash catches it.
- Restore the token budget the same way: if you have been reading full renders, fix the run
  command's summary until the score and the gained/lost sheets are enough.
- **Deployment is not quality work**: memory limits, instance sizes, job APIs and device ports are
  their own tasks with their own measurements, and a cost comparison of alternatives (per item,
  dated list prices, what leaves the machine) is a table in the docs, not a round's report.

## Going to the owner

Go when one of these holds; otherwise keep running the inner loop alone:

- the render (State 2) or the answer key (State 3) needs approval, or a stage's overlay is ready
  - stop after each stage's overlay, not after the whole pipeline
- two iterations without a gain beyond noise
- a fix would add a criterion for what the object *is* - only the owner adds domain rules
- a filter's threshold is in doubt - show the objects only that filter rejects
- the objects look separable: approve sample sub-images and say whether neighbours interact
- a large sample would take long to key: ask whether to key it or keep it as a readability-only
  test, rather than guess
- a version is about to be called final or run on new inputs

**How to ask:** one checkpoint: one image with numbered overlays, one lettered list of the
uncertain items, one before/after table, one status line (`all: 23 full, 26 partial, 37 missed ·
sample6 weakest`), and "what I need from you" as a numbered list at the end. One concrete
question per render ("objects 4, 9 and 12 are rejected only by the elongation filter - are they
real?"); batch rather than interrupt per finding.

**How to report at each exit:** the numbers before and after, what changed, and each remaining
failure with its class and whether it needs the owner (unknowable, hidden, a new sample class) or
a new direction. That last part is what earns the next round of useful feedback instead of a
repeat of the last one.

**How to take the answer:** the owner tends to answer with a rule ("anything touching the edge is
not real") rather than with labels. Encode each rule as a check in the pipeline, a key field or an
invariance test, so the inner loop runs on it without the owner, then return to State 4. Only the
owner supplies object identity, physical facts of the scene (the trapezoid, the hidden author,
the stain that bleeds), key corrections, new sample classes and direction; the method - real
geometry, naive first, uncertain items only, show before using - is this skill's and should not
need saying twice.

## Where the two disciplines differ

| | Microscopy | Phone photo of everyday objects |
|---|---|---|
| Scale and frame | µm/px and channel order from the file's metadata; z and focus per tile; stitched-tile seams | EXIF orientation; no absolute scale without a reference object; perspective, so parallel edges converge |
| Typical invariances | rotation and flip; intensity scale across exposures; channel gain | rotation and perspective; distance; lighting and glare; polarity; upside-down objects |

{"number":234,"title":"Give the NoR Finder page a Google API key for Drive links","body":"The page's "Load → From Google Drive" option reads public Drive links, and it stays greyed out until the site has a Google API key. These steps create one.

- [ ] Create a project named `NoR Finder` → [New project](https://console.cloud.google.com/projectcreate)
- [ ] Enable the Google Drive API → [Drive API](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/drive.googleapis.com)
- [ ] Press Create credentials → API key → [Credentials](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials)
- [ ] Restrict the key: websites `https://missingbulb.github.io/*`, API Google Drive API
- [ ] Paste the key (begins `AIza`) into this issue, or into `apiKey` in [config.js](https://github.com/missingbulb/NoRFinder/edit/main/web/config.js)

**Done when:** on https://missingbulb.github.io/NoRFinder/web/, Load ▾ → From Google Drive opens a box, and pasting the lab's public folder link lists "Left Up- Edited" and the other folders.

## Background

- **Why a key at all.** Drive's plain download link refuses any request a browser marks as coming from another site. The Drive API answers a page on another site only when the page sends an API key. No one signs in, and no consent screen, OAuth client or test users are needed.
- **Why it is safe to paste here.** A browser API key is public by design. The website restriction is what stops anyone else using it, and the API restriction limits it to Drive.
- **What it can read.** Only files and folders shared as "Anyone with the link".
- **What happens next.** Once the key is in `web/config.js`, I release the site and test it against the lab folder.
- **Earlier version.** This issue first asked for an OAuth client and consent screen for Google's file picker. The lighter link-based route replaced that.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/NoRFinder/issues/234","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-09-29T10:08:43Z","updated_at":"2026-09-29T10:31:24Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":226,"title":"Turn on GitHub Pages for the NoR Finder page","body":"Two repository settings that let the NoR Finder page (PR #225) deploy. Nothing in the repo can set them.

- [x] Set Source to "GitHub Actions" → [Pages settings](https://github.com/missingbulb/NoRFinder/settings/pages), under Build and deployment
- [x] Allow the default branch `main` to deploy → [Environments](https://github.com/missingbulb/NoRFinder/settings/environments), open `github-pages`, Deployment branches and tags

## Why

The github-pages pack deploys through `.github/workflows/github-pages-deploy.yml`, which the nightly `github-pages/site-release` task dispatches.

- **Source.** While it is off, `actions/deploy-pages` fails and nothing is served. Done when the first site-release run deploys.
- **Environment branch rule.** While it is off, the environment refuses the deploy job. Done when the deploy job runs instead of waiting on an environment rule. The `github-pages` environment appears once Source is set.

Once both are on and #225 has merged, force the first release instead of waiting for the nightly one:

```
gh workflow run claudinite-scheduler.yml -f wake=github-pages/site-release
```

RAW DIGEST — missingbulb/NoRFinder, 6 merged PRs, window 2026-09-28 09:23 UTC – 2026-09-29 10:23 UTC.

Structural note up front: **zero GitHub review comments/reviews on any of the six PRs** (`get_reviews`/`get_review_comments`/`get_comments` all returned empty for all six). This is a solo-owner repo where Claude Code authors PRs from a Claude-project thread ("Requested by Ariel · project thread" in every body) and the owner (`missingbulb`) merges directly, same session, usually within ~15–60 min of PR creation. So there is no GitHub-side pushback to quote anywhere — all "friction" signal below is inferred from PR-body before/after/how/checks text (which is unusually detailed and self-documents bugs/reworks) and from diff content itself, not from review threads.

=== #221 "Commit the NoR detection work" ===
1. Summary: migrates 3 days of NoR-detection work (finders, scoring lab, labels, ideas ledger, owner criteria, lessons) out of a Claude-project shared folder into the repo (`detection/`), makes paths repo-relative, adds `STATE.md`, promotes owner's NoR criteria to requirements doc R7, folds a project-specific skill into the generic canon skill `image-algorithm-development`.
2. No pushback (no reviews).
3. No revert/rework within the PR; 3 commits are sequential additions (commit, then a provenance-landing commit, then the skill-fold commit).
4. Non-obvious: the PR body states the motivating problem explicitly — "A session started from the repo could see none of it" — i.e. work-in-progress research state living only in a Claude Project's shared folder is invisible to any other session. This directly produced the repo's own local-pack rule "Where the work lives" (`.claudinite/local/packs/nor-finder/RULES.md`), which is already-landed/enforced — not a new candidate.
5. Already-settled: "a Claude project may keep only temporary processing artifacts" — this is the existing nor-finder local rule, already in the mounted RULES.md shown in context. Exclude.

=== #225 "NoR Finder in the browser" ===
1. Summary: ports the existing Python finders to run client-side via Pyodide in a module worker, with a "detect once, filter live" architecture (`detection/interactive.py` re-runs only the cheap checks on stored candidate measurements; a full re-detect is reserved for changing detection-time parameters). Deploys via the canon `github-pages` pack rather than a bespoke workflow.
2/3. No review pushback; no in-PR rework. PR body explicitly flags its own diff breadth: "Diff breadth: besides `web/` and `detection/interactive.py`, this touches `.claudinite/` and `.github/`. That is the pack adoption itself... rather than something this change chose" — i.e. the author pre-empts the "wide diff for a small ask" review concern named in basics/RULES.md, self-justifying via the pack-adoption mechanism.
4. Non-obvious: `web/sw.js` (service worker) is introduced here caching *only third-party code* (Pyodide/CDN/vendor wheels), explicitly never the site's own files, "so a deploy is picked up on the next load" — this exact file gets revisited and tightened twice more in #230 and #235 (see below), i.e. a three-PR progressive rework of the same caching boundary.
5. Already-settled: "never add a workflow that publishes... the site-release task is the one path to production" (github-pages pack rule) — cited/followed here, not new.

=== #228 "New layout, Find Candidates on demand, fixes for red-displayed DAPI, numbering, marks" ===
1. Summary: largest fix-bundle PR (7 commits) — fixes 4 slides failing to load, makes candidate numbers stable across filter changes, makes "remove" persistent and non-destructive, adds busy/progress UI, fixes a dead "measuring lines" checkbox, moves detection from "runs automatically on image load" to an explicit "Find Candidates" button, and restructures the whole page layout.
2. No review comments (none exist), but the PR body itself is candid about a design mistake being corrected: "The page ran the finder as soon as an image loaded" (before) → now on-demand.
3. **Real bug + real rework, in-PR:** commit `8673c1e7` fixes channel loading, and the *very next* commit `e0a3745` ("data/README: the loader compares only the non-green channels for DAPI") tightens the fix further after landing it — a same-PR two-step correction of the same root cause.
   - Root cause (from `detection/naive_nor.py` diff): the old loader picked DAPI as `argmax(blobbiness)` across **all three** channels, then separately looked up red/green channel indices **by their ImageJ display LUT colour**, and asserted DAPI's index wasn't the red or green index. In files where DAPI happens to be *displayed red*, that assert always fires ("DAPI detected on a green/red channel"), because display colour was being used as a proxy for channel *role*. Fix: Caspr's index is still taken from the green LUT (a real invariant, confirmed data-README fact across all 55 files), but DAPI is now chosen as the blobbiest of **only the two non-green channels**, and Nav is whatever remains — display colour is never used to identify DAPI or Nav1.6, only to identify Caspr. This also incidentally fixed the one file (`Up Middle.../Slice3_up_middle2.tif`) whose blob-size heuristic previously failed because a bright Caspr tissue edge outscored real nuclei when compared against all 3 channels instead of just the 2 candidates.
   - This is a strong non-obvious-reason/small-diff candidate: **display colour (a rendering choice) and channel role (a biological identity) are different axes, and conflating them for even one of three channels silently breaks a whole file class.**
4. See point 3 — same item.
5. Already-settled: nothing new; uses the existing `MAIN` finder-settings convention and existing filter/check architecture from `nor3.py`/`interactive.py`.

=== #230 "Fixed frame with scrolling columns, 1cm footer with site version" ===
1. Summary: makes the page frame fixed-height (header/columns/1cm-footer fill the window, only columns scroll) instead of whole-page-scroll; adds the site version to the footer via the newly-adopted `public-website` pack's version-stamp mechanism; tightens the service worker.
2/3. No review comments. Notable candid uncertainty in the PR body itself: "Stale files: after the last release, a browser could keep the previous stylesheet for a few minutes and show it with the new page... I infer that is why it showed huge; **I did not reproduce it**." — a fix shipped for a hypothesized (not confirmed) root cause of a real user-observed symptom (logo showing huge in Ariel's browser). This directly conflicts with the basics-pack discipline of "never document/recommend a path you haven't run" / "verify against a real run" — worth flagging since the fix (`sw.js` revalidating the site's own files with `cache: "no-cache"`, plus explicit width/height on the logo SVG so no browser falls back to a default size) is plausible but explicitly unverified against the actual failure.
4. Non-obvious: the version stamp is deliberately sourced from `package.json` via the `public-website` pack's `bump-version.mjs --stamp-only`, never hand-typed — this is the general public-website pack rule already in context (not new), but this PR is the concrete instance of adopting it for this repo. Not a new candidate.
5. Already-settled: the whole version-stamping mechanism is the public-website pack's existing rule (already shown in RULES.md context) — exclude.

=== #232 "Tidier toolbar, footer, spacing; help for every finder/setting; v0.10928.x" ===
1. Summary: UI/spacing consistency pass (one `--pad`/`--r-panel`/`--r-ctl`/`--r-chip` scale used everywhere), icon-only theme toggle, renamed layer labels (Nav1.6/Caspr/DAPI instead of red/green/blue), and — the substantive piece — adds `detection/finder_help.py` with per-finder `ABOUT` text and per-setting `HELP` text, surfaced on the page as a "?" tooltip.
2/3. No review comments; no in-PR rework.
4. **Non-obvious, durable-looking mechanism:** a new test, `test_every_finder_and_setting_is_explained` in `tests/test_interactive.py`, walks every finder's `describe()` output and asserts every shown detection param and every shown filter param has a `HELP` entry, and every finder has a non-empty `ABOUT`. PR body: "A new test... fails when a finder or any setting the page shows has no explanation, so a new setting must come with one. I watched it fail on a removed entry." This is a **generic, reusable pattern**: a coverage test that diffs "what the UI actually surfaces" against "what has been documented for the user," so documentation can't silently lag behind new settings/finders.   3. No revert/rework within the PR; 3 commits are sequential additions (commit, then a provenance-landing commit, then the skill-fold commit).
  4. Non-obvious: the PR body states the motivating problem explicitly — "A session started from the repo could see none of it" — i.e. work-in-progress research state living only in a Claude Project's shared folder is invisible to any other session. This directly produced the repo's own local-pack rule "Where the work lives" (`.claudinite/local/packs/nor-finder/RULES.md`), which is already-landed/enforced — not a new candidate.
  5. Already-settled: "a Claude project may keep only temporary processing artifacts" — this is the existing nor-finder local rule, already in the mounted RULES.md shown in context. Exclude.
  
  === #225 "NoR Finder in the browser" ===
  1. Summary: ports the existing Python finders to run client-side via Pyodide in a module worker, with a "detect once, filter live" architecture (`detection/interactive.py` re-runs only the cheap checks on stored candidate measurements; a full re-detect is reserved for changing detection-time parameters). Deploys via the canon `github-pages` pack rather than a bespoke workflow.
  2/3. No review pushback; no in-PR rework. PR body explicitly flags its own diff breadth: "Diff breadth: besides `web/` and `detection/interactive.py`, this touches `.claudinite/` and `.github/`. That is the pack adoption itself... rather than something this change chose" — i.e. the author pre-empts the "wide diff for a small ask" review concern named in basics/RULES.md, self-justifying via the pack-adoption mechanism.
  4. Non-obvious: `web/sw.js` (service worker) is introduced here caching *only third-party code* (Pyodide/CDN/vendor wheels), explicitly never the site's own files, "so a deploy is picked up on the next load" — this exact file gets revisited and tightened twice more in #230 and #235 (see below), i.e. a three-PR progressive rework of the same caching boundary.
  5. Already-settled: "never add a workflow that publishes... the site-release task is the one path to production" (github-pages pack rule) — cited/followed here, not new.
  
  === #228 "New layout, Find Candidates on demand, fixes for red-displayed DAPI, numbering, marks" ===
  1. Summary: largest fix-bundle PR (7 commits) — fixes 4 slides failing to load, makes candidate numbers stable across filter changes, makes "remove" persistent and non-destructive, adds busy/progress UI, fixes a dead "measuring lines" checkbox, moves detection from "runs automatically on image load" to an explicit "Find Candidates" button, and restructures the whole page layout.
  2. No review comments (none exist), but the PR body itself is candid about a design mistake being corrected: "The page ran the finder as soon as an image loaded" (before) → now on-demand.
  3. **Real bug + real rework, in-PR:** commit `8673c1e7` fixes channel loading, and the *very next* commit `e0a3745` ("data/README: the loader compares only the non-green channels for DAPI") tightens the fix further after landing it — a same-PR two-step correction of the same root cause.
     - Root cause (from `detection/naive_nor.py` diff): the old loader picked DAPI as `argmax(blobbiness)` across **all three** channels, then separately looked up red/green channel indices **by their ImageJ display LUT colour**, and asserted DAPI's index wasn't the red or green index. In files where DAPI happens to be *displayed red*, that assert always fires ("DAPI detected on a green/red channel"), because display colour was being used as a proxy for channel *role*. Fix: Caspr's index is still taken from the green LUT (a real invariant, confirmed data-README fact across all 55 files), but DAPI is now chosen as the blobbiest of **only the two non-green channels**, and Nav is whatever remains — display colour is never used to identify DAPI or Nav1.6, only to identify Caspr. This also incidentally fixed the one file (`Up Middle.../Slice3_up_middle2.tif`) whose blob-size heuristic previously failed because a bright Caspr tissue edge outscored real nuclei when compared against all 3 channels instead of just the 2 candidates.
     - This is a strong non-obvious-reason/small-diff candidate: **display colour (a rendering choice) and channel role (a biological identity) are different axes, and conflating them for even one of three channels silently breaks a whole file class.**
  4. See point 3 — same item.
  5. Already-settled: nothing new; uses the existing `MAIN` finder-settings convention and existing filter/check architecture from `nor3.py`/`interactive.py`.

I infer that is why it showed huge; **I did not reproduce it**." — a fix shipped for a hypothesized (not confirmed) root cause of a real user-observed symptom (logo showing huge in Ariel's browser).   4. Non-obvious: the version stamp is deliberately sourced from `package.json` via the `public-website` pack's `bump-version.mjs --stamp-only`, never hand-typed — this is the general public-website pack rule already in context (not new), but this PR is the concrete instance of adopting it for this repo. Not a new candidate.
  5. Already-settled: the whole version-stamping mechanism is the public-website pack's existing rule (already shown in RULES.md context) — exclude.
  
  === #232 "Tidier toolbar, footer, spacing; help for every finder/setting; v0.10928.x" ===
  1. Summary: UI/spacing consistency pass (one `--pad`/`--r-panel`/`--r-ctl`/`--r-chip` scale used everywhere), icon-only theme toggle, renamed layer labels (Nav1.6/Caspr/DAPI instead of red/green/blue), and — the substantive piece — adds `detection/finder_help.py` with per-finder `ABOUT` text and per-setting `HELP` text, surfaced on the page as a "?" tooltip.
  2/3. No review comments; no in-PR rework.
  4. **Non-obvious, durable-looking mechanism:** a new test, `test_every_finder_and_setting_is_explained` in `tests/test_interactive.py`, walks every finder's `describe()` output and asserts every shown detection param and every shown filter param has a `HELP` entry, and every finder has a non-empty `ABOUT`. PR body: "A new test... fails when a finder or any setting the page shows has no explanation, so a new setting must come with one. I watched it fail on a removed entry." This is a **generic, reusable pattern**: a coverage test that diffs "what the UI actually surfaces" against "what has been documented for the user," so documentation can't silently lag behind new settings/finders. This is a candidate for a durable lesson (goes beyond this one window — it's a generalizable technique for keeping user-facing help text from rotting, not a fact about this codebase).
     - Also non-obvious: `package.json` version is deliberately dropped from `1.10928.1` to `0.10928.1` in this PR, with the PR body explaining why: "The release carries the major number over from `package.json`, so setting it to 0 there... moves later releases to 0.x." This is a real, easy-to-get-backwards mechanic of the public-website pack's versioning (the release process reads the major version forward from what's committed) — but it's describing an already-existing mechanism of that pack, not a new rule to land here; flagging only because the "why" is genuinely non-obvious from the one-line diff (`"version": "1.10928.1"` → `"0.10928.1"`) alone.
  5. Already-settled: nothing new architecturally.
  
  === #235 "Page round 3: navigation, selection, item views, ground truth" ===
  1. Summary: biggest page-behavior PR — drag-to-pan/scroll-to-zoom/scroll-sideways-to-step-candidates navigation, click-to-select with a right-bar detail card (replacing "click a marking flips its verdict"), splits the single finalist list into Finalists/Rejected views with per-candidate rejection-reason breakdown, adds a ground-truth JSON export/import path consumed by the Python lab (`nor_lab.py --labels`), per-filter "what it rejects alone" counts, resizable side panels, and Google-Drive image loading (`web/drive.js`, `web/config.js`).
  2/3. No review comments. But two **real, non-obvious bug fixes bundled into this PR**, each independently small-diff/non-obvious-reason:
     a. **`detection/nor3.py` `judge()`**: changed `for k in (order or ORDER):` → `for k in (ORDER if order is None else order):`. The PR body states this directly: "`nor3.judge` no longer treats an empty order as 'all checks'." Root cause: Python's `x or default` treats an explicitly-passed empty list the same as "not passed," so a caller that means "turn every check off" (`order=[]`) was silently getting "run every check" instead — a classic None-vs-falsy conflation bug. This is a strong, generalizable, reusable code-correctness lesson (distinct from — but a specific instance of — the "unknown is a state of its own" rule already in basics/RULES.md; here it's specifically about the `x or default` idiom swallowing meaningful falsy/empty values in Python).
     b. **`web/sw.js`** tightened a third time (see #225, #230 above): now explicitly excludes user-loaded files (e.g. a file read from Google Drive) from the code cache, keeping the cache scoped to "the third-party code the page runs." Comment added: "never a user's own files, such as one read from Google Drive." This is the third distinct revision of the same caching-boundary file across three PRs in the window — each round narrowing what "the site's own stuff" means (own code vs. third-party code vs. user data) as new load paths were added. That's a real multi-round-redesign signal, spread across PRs rather than within one.
  4. Also worth flagging: `tests/test_interactive.py` gained `test_every_reason_has_its_own_letter_and_title`, mirroring #232's "every setting must be explained" test but for rejection-reason letters/titles — same reusable "UI-surface coverage test" pattern as #232, applied a second time to a second surface (reasons vs. settings). Reinforces that as a real recurring technique rather than a one-off.
  5. Already-settled: nothing new architecturally beyond what the pattern above already covers.
  
  **Cross-PR / issue-level finding worth flagging** (found while checking referenced issue #234, opened same day as #235, still open): issue #234 ("Give the NoR Finder page a Google API key for Drive links") describes, and asks the owner to set up, a **link-based / API-key-only** Drive integration, and explicitly says: *"Earlier version. This issue first asked for an OAuth client and consent screen for Google's file picker. The lighter link-based route replaced that."* But the code actually merged in #235 (`web/drive.js`, `web/config.js`) implements exactly the OAuth-consent + Google Picker flow the issue says was replaced: `google.accounts.oauth2.initTokenClient(...)`, `google.picker.PickerBuilder()`, and `NOR_CONFIG.google` requiring `apiKey`, `clientId`, **and** `appId` — three values, only one of which (`apiKey`) issue #234's checklist actually asks the owner to obtain and paste in. So the human-facing setup issue under-specifies what the shipped code needs (no mention of getting/setting `clientId` or `appId`), and its own "earlier version" note appears to describe an approach that was *not* actually the one shipped. This looks like real drift between an issue's narrative and the code that landed in the same window — a candidate worth someone checking against the current state of #234/config.js in the live repo.
  
  === Candidate signals (flagging generously per instructions; not my recommendation on inclusion) ===
  1. **`x or default` silently swallows a meaningful empty/falsy value in Python** — `nor3.judge`'s `order or ORDER` bug (#235). Generalizable Python-correctness lesson, not project-specific. Possibly already covered by basics/RULES.md's "Handling a value that can be unknown" (that rule is about zero/empty-string/None conflation in data; this is the same shape but specifically the `or`-fallback idiom in control flow) — flag for a dedupe check against that rule.
  2. **UI-surface coverage test pattern**: a test that enumerates everything the UI actually shows (every finder, every setting, every rejection-reason letter) and asserts each has required accompanying explanatory text, so help text can't drift out of sync with new settings (#232, reused in #235). Generalizable beyond this repo.
  3. **Conflating a display/rendering attribute with a semantic/identity attribute for only one case among several** silently breaks the other cases (#228's DAPI-by-display-colour bug: green was safely identified by LUT colour as an invariant, but red/blue were not, so files with an unusual DAPI display colour broke). Generalizable "domain assumption" lesson, arguably already covered by research-project pack's "keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode" — flag for dedupe check.
  4. **Shipping a stale-cache fix for a symptom the author explicitly did not reproduce** (#230: "I did not reproduce it"). Possible tension with basics/RULES.md "verify... against a real run" / "don't document a path you haven't run" — flag as a possible gap in how that rule is currently interpreted (it may already cover this, or may need to explicitly address "fixing a hypothesized cause of an unreproduced symptom").
  5. **A service-worker/cache-boundary file revised three separate times across three separate PRs** (#225 → #230 → #235), each time narrowing the definition of "cacheable" as new data-loading paths were added (own code → +revalidation of own files → −user-loaded files). Possibly indicates a "define the caching boundary by exhaustive membership test up front" lesson, or may just be organic feature growth — flag as weak/uncertain signal.
  6. **Issue text and shipped code disagreeing** on which Google auth flow was used (#234 vs #235's `drive.js`), with the issue's setup checklist missing two of three required config values. Flag as a possible pattern worth a mechanism (e.g., a check that a config object's required keys are all named in the issue/doc that asks a human to fill them) — relates to `writing-handover-issues` skill territory, worth cross-checking there.

245	- **Moving around the image.** Dragging moves the image; scrolling up and down zooms around the
246	  pointer in small steps; scrolling sideways steps to the previous or next candidate. The Show
247	  menu switches accepted and rejected markings on and off, each with its own line width and colour,
248	  and the candidate numbers, the rejection letters and the measuring lines (remembered).
249	- **One selected candidate.** Clicking a candidate selects it (a thin white ring) and clicking it
250	  again deselects it. Its card sits in the right bar with buttons to the previous and next
251	  candidate by number. Decisions are made on cards, not by clicking the image: a finalist can be
252	  rejected, always accepted, or have its lengths approved; a rejected one can be accepted, and one
253	  rejected by the user restored.
254	- **Filters are live dials.** Every check in `nor3.CHECKS`, the nucleus rule (N) and
255	  one-pixel-per-NoR (O) is a control that can be switched off. Each shows a letter, a one- or
256	  two-word title and a line saying what it means (the page's own names, from
257	  `detection/finder_help.py`; the lab's review sheets keep theirs), and how many candidates it
258	  rejects by itself, whatever the other filters do. Each of its parameters is a dial, and
259	  every marking on the image follows it at once. A check added to `CHECKS` becomes a control with
260	  no page change.
261	- **Detection settings are dials too.** They re-run the finder, and the page says that this takes
262	  time. Each finder names its main settings (its function's `MAIN`), shown first; every setting is
263	  under a collapsed Advanced box. Each finder shows a few sentences on how it works, and every setting and
264	  filter value has a ? that says what it does (`detection/finder_help.py`; the test fails when one
265	  is missing).
266	- **All finders are offered.** Traffic light is the default.
267	- **The blue mask is only a filter.** No finder on the page blanks nuclei before finding.
268	- **The item views.** Two views: the finalists and the rejected, each candidate cropped on a card.
269	  A rejected card names every filter that rejects it by itself, or says the user rejected it. An
270	  Options menu (remembered) sets the crop's context padding, turns each crop so the NoR lies level
271	  (on at first), and shows or hides the NoR borders, the measurement bars, the lengths on the crop,
272	  the lengths on the card and the length adjusters (on at first). The adjusters drag the ends of
273	  the green-to-green length and the red length; the new lengths show on the image, the card, the
274	  summary and the downloads. The measurements of the finalists are summarised in the right bar.

  two-word title and a line saying what it means (the page's own names, from
  `detection/finder_help.py`; the lab's review sheets keep theirs), and how many candidates it
  rejects by itself, whatever the other filters do. Each of its parameters is a dial, and
  every marking on the image follows it at once. A check added to `CHECKS` becomes a control with
  no page change.

  time. Each finder names its main settings (its function's `MAIN`), shown first; every setting is
  under a collapsed Advanced box. Each finder shows a few sentences on how it works, and every setting and
  filter value has a ? that says what it does (`detection/finder_help.py`; the test fails when one
  is missing).

- **The blue mask is only a filter.** No finder on the page blanks nuclei before finding.
- **The item views.** Two views: the finalists and the rejected, each candidate cropped on a card.
  A rejected card names every filter that rejects it by itself, or says the user rejected it. An
  Options menu (remembered) sets the crop's context padding, turns each crop so the NoR lies level
  (on at first), and shows or hides the NoR borders, the measurement bars, the lengths on the crop,
  the lengths on the card and the length adjusters (on at first). The adjusters drag the ends of
  the green-to-green length and the red length; the new lengths show on the image, the card, the
  summary and the downloads. The measurements of the finalists are summarised in the right bar.

## Friction digest

**1. `ToolSearch` called before its gating skill is loaded — recurs in essentially every automated session.**
Source: issue-67, issue-68, issue-66, issue-74 (2026-09-13); pr-224, pr-241 (2026-09-28/29). In every one of these queue-fired sessions, the agent's very first `ToolSearch` call is blocked by the PreToolUse hook (`skill-not-loaded-for-call ToolSearch needs searching-for-a-tool`), then it loads the `searching-for-a-tool` skill and retries successfully. This is 100% reproducible at session start across a 16-day span (still happening on 09-29, the newest capture), costing one wasted tool call + a full round trip per session. Same shape recurs for two other skill-gated tools within the same sessions: `Bash` blocked pending the `committing` skill (issue-74) and `mcp__github__merge_pull_request` blocked pending `merge-to-main` (issue-74, pr-241) — each a once-per-session, same-pattern block-then-load-then-retry.
Durability: high — this is a structural, session-start cost that repeats on nearly every automated work-item session over the full window sampled (7 of 9 logs read touch it directly), not a one-off.

**2. Blind `sleep` reached for before `Monitor`, when waiting on a CI check.**
Source: pr-224 (2026-09-28T16:27:13Z, `sleep 30` after `enable_pr_auto_merge` reported "unstable status"); pr-241 (2026-09-29T10:32:44Z, `sleep 60`, same trigger). Both blocked by the harness ("Blocked: standalone sleep… use Monitor with an until-loop"). Recovery differed: pr-224 switched to `Monitor` with a while-loop, did other work while waiting, and got notified ~17s later when the check went green (good recovery, minimal loss). pr-241 did *not* use `Monitor` — it ran one unrelated Bash command, then just re-polled `pull_request_read` once manually ~25s later, which happened to have already gone green. Total wall time lost in both cases was small (~20–25s), but the pattern — reach for `sleep` first, get blocked, only sometimes correct to `Monitor` — recurs across two different sessions six days apart.
Durability: medium — small individual cost, but a repeated first-instinct-is-wrong pattern at the exact same trigger point (auto-merge reporting "unstable").

**3. Redundant re-run of `converge-item.mjs` with an unchanged command.**
Source: issue-237 (2026-09-29). The script was run at 10:34:47Z and returned a complete, correct transition plan at 10:34:49Z. The agent then read `converge-item.mjs`'s own source (seemingly to double-check something) and re-ran the *identical* command at 10:35:23Z, getting the identical output — ~40s and one full script execution wasted for no behavior change. Checked across the other 8 logs: only issue-237 shows 2 `converge-item.mjs` invocations; every other converge call in both windows is single-shot. 
Durability: low — looks like a one-off hesitation rather than a recurring habit; flagging per instructions but this alone probably doesn't clear the bar.

**4. Repeatedly ending a unit of work without pushing — caught 3× by the Stop hook in one session.**
Source: pr-232 (2026-09-28), an interactive/manual (non-queue-fired) research session on browser-based NoR detection. At 17:02:09Z, 17:42:45Z and 18:39:01Z the Stop hook (`stop-hook-git-check.sh`) fired "Branch '<name>' has N unpushed commit(s) and no remote branch. Please push." for three different work branches (`browser-feasibility`, `fix-channels-numbers`, `toolbar-polish`) in the same session. Each time the agent pushed and only then could actually stop. No other log in either window shows this message, so it's confined to this one long interactive session, but it recurred three separate times inside it — the agent's habit of trying to end a "unit of work" without pushing first is consistent, only corrected by the existing hook rather than avoided.
Durability: medium — matches an already-written rule (basics.md "Finishing a unit of work — leave it committed and pushed") that a hook already enforces; the friction is that the agent needs the hook's push-back every single time rather than pushing proactively per branch.

**5. Long visual-iteration session exhausted its context window.**
Source: pr-232 (2026-09-28, 16:57:44Z–~18:39:01Z, ~1h41m). This single interactive session (comparing a JS-port vs Pyodide browser approach for NoR detection, per the research-project pack's show-a-comparison rule) read 22 separate image tool-results (screenshots, several 400–620KB each), and around 18:04:27Z the conversation had to be auto-continued after running out of context. No obviously redundant screenshots were found (each capture followed a real code/render change), so this looks like the legitimate cost of a rule-mandated visual-iteration workflow rather than a bug — flagging it as observed friction, but I don't think it clears the bar as an actionable lesson without more sessions showing the same exhaustion pattern.
Durability: low-to-medium, mostly informational — this is likely an accepted cost of the research-project pack's "show a rendered comparison" requirement rather than a fixable inefficiency.

## What I did not find
No repeated user-asked efficiency/process questions across sessions (the automated sessions have no interactive user in the loop — they're queue-fired against `queue/instructions.md`), no misunderstanding/correction round-trips with a human, and no evidence of a heavy-tool-over-light-tool substitution beyond the ToolSearch-gate pattern already noted in #1. Nothing else in the two windows rose above one-off noise.

input.title: Drive setup checklist (#234) doesn't mention clientId and appId, which drive.js requires
input.body:
`web/drive.js`'s `configured()` gates the "Load → From Google Drive" option on `apiKey && clientId && appId` all three, and uses `clientId` for `google.accounts.oauth2.initTokenClient` (a consent prompt) and `appId` for `google.picker.PickerBuilder().setAppId(...)`.

#234's checklist only asks for `apiKey`, and its own "Earlier version" note says the OAuth-client/consent-screen route was replaced by "the lighter link-based route" — but the code actually shipped in #235 (`web/drive.js`) is the OAuth-consent + Picker flow, not a plain API-key-only fetch. Pasting only `apiKey` per the current checklist would leave `configured()` false and the option greyed out.

Refs #234, #235.
